writing.explanation:
A problem is a good match for Bitmask Enumeration when it asks for small subsets, permissions, feature combinations. Here the concrete task is: Return masks whose selected values sum to 5. The visible input `values=[1,2,4]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Check number size, sign, and modulus assumptions before using a shortcut; not every inverse or division exists. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Use each bit as an include/exclude choice for one item. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? An arithmetic or bitwise transformation relies on an identity. Write that identity and the domain in which it holds. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(2^n*n) time · O(1) state excluding output; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `5` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Test zero, one, powers of two, maximum input size, and overflow or underflow around intermediate products. Use explicit integer widths and checked arithmetic when input bounds require them. Distinguish bit positions from numeric values. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
